title: Seeing the board without the pieces
outcomes: Names the colour of a square from its name
Gives the squares a knight reaches in one and in two jumps, and says when a square cannot be reached
Names the squares of a long diagonal
Plans a short routine of their own to train board vision without a board

steps.text: A way to train board vision: hold a position as **a list of pieces and the squares they attack**. Train the small parts first. **Colour from the name:** a1 is dark; add the file number (a=1 to h=8) and the rank, and an even sum is dark. Say the answer **before** you look at the board; looking is how you check, not how you answer.

steps.caption: A knight on b1. The lit squares are its first jump. Watch the colours of the squares it lands on.

line.say: From the light square b1 the knight jumps to c3, a dark square.
Black makes a waiting move with the king.
From c3 it jumps to e4, light again. A knight changes colour on every jump.

claims.statement: The knight on b1 attacks exactly a3, c3 and d2.
From c3 the knight attacks e4.

steps.text: This is easiest while the line is **short** and you **re-anchor** after each move by saying what is attacked now. A slip to watch for as lines get longer: counting a piece that was captured a move ago. **Rule of thumb:** after every capture, say the new list of pieces aloud before going on. A knight always changes square colour, which rules out half the squares at once.

steps.title: Can the knight get there?
steps.prompt: Count the jumps in your head first. Predict, then check.

Choose a two-minute drill you can do without a board, away from the app: for example name the colour of ten squares from a list, or name the squares a knight reaches in two jumps from each corner. Score it today as a baseline.
